title: Insurance Capital Standards Clarification Act of 2014
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was passed by the Senate on June 3, 2014. The summary of that version is repeated here.)

Insurance Capital Standards Clarification Act of 2014 - Amends the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (Dodd-Frank) concerning establishment of minimum leverage and minimum risk-based capital requirements on a consolidated basis for a depository institution holding company or a nonbank financial company supervised by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.

States that federal banking agencies shall not be required to subject any person to such minimum capital requirements, to the extent that such person either: (1) acts in its capacity as a regulated insurance entity regulated by a state insurance regulator, or (2) is a regulated foreign subsidiary engaged in the business of insurance (including a regulated foreign affiliate of such subsidiary).

States that a Board-supervised depository institution holding company or nonbank financial company engaged in the insurance business and regulated by either a state insurance regulator or the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, and which files its holding company financial statements using only Statutory Accounting Principles pursuant to state law, shall not be required by the Board, under this Act or the Home Owners' Loan Act (HOLA), to prepare such financial statements in accordance with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles.

Declares that nothing in this Act shall: (1) limit Board authority to conduct any regulatory or supervisory activity of either a depository institution holding company or a non-bank financial company under Board jurisdiction, including the collecting or reporting of any information on an entity or group-wide basis; or (2) excuse the Board from its obligations to comply with Dodd-Frank requirements regarding examination of nonbank financial companies and HOLA requirements regarding examination of savings and loan holding companies.

summary.headline: This law tells the Federal Reserve not to apply certain bank-style capital rules to insurance companies regulated by states, and lets some insurance-focused holding companies use state accounting rules.
summary.what_it_does: It amends the Dodd-Frank Act so that federal banking agencies do not have to apply minimum leverage and risk-based capital requirements, on a consolidated basis, to people or companies acting as state-regulated insurers or to regulated foreign insurance subsidiaries. It also says that a Federal Reserve-supervised holding company in the insurance business, regulated by a state insurance regulator or the NAIC, can file its financial statements under Statutory Accounting Principles instead of GAAP. The law states that the Federal Reserve keeps its full power to supervise and collect information, and that its examination duties remain unchanged.

who_it_affects.group: Insurance companies regulated by state insurance regulators
who_it_affects.how: They are not required to meet the federal bank-style minimum capital requirements on a consolidated basis for their insurance activities.

who_it_affects.group: Foreign insurance subsidiaries of covered holding companies
who_it_affects.how: Regulated foreign subsidiaries engaged in insurance, and their regulated foreign affiliates, are likewise exempt from those consolidated capital requirements.

who_it_affects.group: Depository institution holding companies and nonbank financial companies supervised by the Federal Reserve that are in the insurance business
who_it_affects.how: They may file holding company financial statements under state Statutory Accounting Principles rather than GAAP, though the Federal Reserve can still collect information on a group-wide basis.

who_it_affects.group: Federal Reserve and other federal banking agencies
who_it_affects.how: They do not have to apply these consolidated capital requirements to the covered insurance entities, but they keep their supervisory and examination authority.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Signed into law on December 18, 2014, with no separate delayed effective date stated in the summary.
